name: Aisha Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I replace rotten sill timber and fit new window boards at the East Road flats. I'm fifty-eight, have a trade certificate and can take a normal room from measurement to finish, though I still ask for help when the wall itself is moving. My partner Niko cooks at a café that closes some winter evenings, and our adult children live in other towns. My site wage is low, we have about three weeks of expenses saved, and there are few local firms doing this work. I use an AI assistant every day to organise window measurements and find fitting instructions, then check the wall and drawing myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the assistant helps me make a clean sill list, so I hope modest AI stays a useful tool in our hands. I would also say a faster list does not make this builder pay more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am worried about winter money before any new machine arrives. Niko's café loses evenings in cold months, and three weeks of savings cannot carry us through a site pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting window boards and checking my AI list against each room. In the first year I'd send the site manager a weekly record of delayed materials and ask about the next paid block before this one ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel grateful for a useful tool and anxious about the wage packet. A saved hour means little if it turns into an unpaid hour instead of another paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake did the assistant make recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It copied the width from flat six into flat nine, where the old wall is narrower. I noticed because I had marked the sill with chalk before opening my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why record delayed materials?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The manager tends to call a gap 'weather' even when the timber order is late. I want the dates written down before the next pay discussion.

say: I'd value a **clean sill list** made with checked AI.
I'd say faster lists do not raise **low site pay** by themselves.
think: Niko's **winter café hours** are uncertain before technology changes.
Our **three-week savings** cannot absorb a long site pause.
do: Keep fitting **window boards** and checking AI measurements room by room.
Send **material-delay dates** to the site manager and request the next block date.
feel: **Grateful and anxious** as tools save time but paid hours remain thin.
S0.quote: A saved hour means little if it turns into an unpaid hour instead of another paid job.
fieldNote: Aisha's daily AI use meets a **chalk-marked sill**, which caught a copied measurement error.
Her concern is whether saved time becomes **paid work**, given café closures and only three weeks saved.

steps.text: Keep fitting paid window boards at East Road
Use AI window lists with chalk and drawing checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site manager that buying software should be tested with the people who carry the new boards up the stairs. I would ask to see one order from the drawing to the room before any worker loses hours over a missed item.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking jobs in the office may shrink, and our repair blocks could be booked less steadily. I can learn a new screen quickly, but there are only a few firms nearby and our account cannot wait through weeks without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the buyer to let me test the ordering tool on a window block and record which parts arrive late. During the first year I'll keep taking paid fitting shifts, and if the next block slips I'll apply to the two local maintenance crews and stop the weekly takeaway with Niko.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about the system and anxious about its effect on our dates. I would rather catch one missing sill board early than hear later that the software marked everything complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The board sizes, fixings, promised delivery and how many paid hours a late item costs. A green mark on the screen is not the same as timber on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on private window repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might take a small paid weekend repair if I had the right materials and insurance, but I won't promise a side business from an empty pocket. The local maintenance posts are a clearer first call.

say: I'd demand a **room-to-delivery trial** before ordering software changes paid hours.
I'd ask the buyer to count late parts and **worker time**.
think: Fewer office staff could bring **uneven repair blocks**.
Fast learning cannot cover **weeks without pay** when few firms hire.
do: Test the **window ordering tool** and record late parts.
Keep **paid fitting shifts** and apply to maintenance if a block slips.
Stop **weekly takeaways** if site work is delayed.
feel: **Curious and anxious** about a tool that could hide unpaid waiting.
S1.quote: A green mark on the screen is not the same as timber on the floor.
fieldNote: Aisha's test includes **paid hours lost** to a late component, not only whether the order appears complete.
She mentions private repairs but makes **no firm side-income plan** without materials and insurance.

steps.text: Test the AI ordering tool on a real window block
Apply to two maintenance crews if the next block slips
Stop weekly takeaways if site work is delayed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI in 2028 could take the drawings and ordering, while robots able to fit windows come around 2031. I would ask for a site test that includes a rotten wall, not a perfect demonstration room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when office work changes and sixty-three when a robot could take my sill fitting. Niko's winter café wage cannot replace this low site pay, and three weeks saved would go before I found much time to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll test the digital window checker on an awkward flat and ask the manager for the next block dates in writing. In 2029 I'll keep taking paid window shifts, apply to the two reachable repair teams if hours fall, and enrol in a building-inspection course only if it includes paid placement close enough for the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by the speed but I am already looking for a bridge. Knowing how to use AI today may help with the plans, yet it will not keep my hands in work after a capable robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to spot damp timber, and a paid inspection placement could use that skill while I learn the reporting side. I do not claim inspection is safe forever if thinking AI is that good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the robot test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see it find rot, stop when the wall moves and leave a fixing that passes a load check. A beautiful new frame on a perfect wall tells me very little.

say: I'd separate **2028 drawings** from 2031 hands-on window robots.
I'd insist on a **rotten-wall trial** before site use.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take the sill-fitting wage we need.
Our **three-week reserve** and Niko's café hours leave little retraining time.
do: Test the **digital checker** and demand written block dates.
Keep **paid window shifts** in 2029 and apply if hours fall.
Enrol only in **paid local inspection training**.
feel: **Frightened**, but actively seeking a paid bridge.
S2.quote: Knowing how to use AI today may help with the plans, yet it will not keep my hands in work after a capable robot arrives.
fieldNote: Aisha distinguishes her **current AI skill** from the later threat to physical window fitting.
Her inspection idea is a **paid conditional placement**, with no claim that it remains safe after AGI.

steps.text: Test the digital window checker on a damaged flat
Keep taking paid window shifts in 2029
Apply to two reachable repair teams if hours fall
Enrol in inspection training only with a paid reachable placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to show a machine more than a tidy new wall. I would ask for a written record of damaged-wall tests and paid chances for workers to learn the new inspection tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots can fit windows. That is more time to earn, but low pay and winter café closures mean I cannot promise a retirement fund by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking East Road work and use my AI measurements with the chalk marks on each sill. In 2032 I'd take paid repair shifts if offered, ask the manager for the coming block dates and apply to nearby maintenance posts if a fortnight is blank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to prepare for the machines and still uneasy about next winter's bills. Extra years matter only if the jobs in them are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your savings on a new course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, three weeks of bills is not course money. I'd enrol only in a funded placement with a wage, because a training promise cannot pay the café's shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you save now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After a full month I could put a small sum aside, but I will not claim a fixed amount every month. I need to see the site calendar first.

say: I'd ask for **damaged-wall tests** and paid learning time.
I'd use five years to inspect **real machine records**.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots could reach window work before we can retire.
Winter café gaps and **low site pay** limit the benefit of extra time.
do: Keep **paid East Road work** and checked AI measurements.
Apply to **maintenance posts** after a blank fortnight.
feel: More **prepared for machines**, still uneasy about bills.
S3.quote: Extra years matter only if the jobs in them are paid.
fieldNote: Aisha's **five-year plan** centers on recorded machine tests and continuing paid repair work.
With three weeks saved, she treats **funded training** as the only viable route into a new role.

steps.text: Keep taking paid window repair shifts in 2032
Use AI measurements against chalk marks on each sill
Apply to nearby maintenance posts after a blank fortnight
Enrol in inspection training only if a funded paid placement is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives workers time to test robots on real old buildings and to teach younger fitters how to spot hidden rot. I would still ask who pays for a failed fixing when the machine leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots can fit windows. I may still need paid repair work then; nothing about today's low rate and tiny account lets me assume I will have retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid sill work and using checked AI lists while sites are open. In 2037 I'd take lighter paid window repairs if my knees permit, and Niko and I would count actual wages and bills before I stopped looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about robots so far away, yet anxious about the next slow café winter. A long warning cannot be spent on this month's electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your adult children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own bills, and I would rather visit than ask for money. We need a plan based on wages Niko and I actually earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm sequence of paid repair blocks would let us move one extra week of expenses into savings. Then I could test tools without every missed shift landing straight on the bill pile.

say: I'd seek **real old-building tests** over the decade.
I'd teach workers to spot **hidden rot** before trusting robot fittings.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid sill repairs.
At **seventy-one**, low pay and thin savings make retirement uncertain.
do: Keep **paid sill work** and checked AI lists.
Take **lighter repairs in 2037** if income is needed.
Count **wages and bills** with Niko before leaving work.
feel: **Anxious about current income**, calm about distant site robots.
S4.quote: A long warning cannot be spent on this month's electricity.
fieldNote: The **long robot horizon** does not ease present café closures and low site pay.
Aisha continues **paid repair plans** if necessary at sixty-eight and leaves adult children outside the budget.

steps.text: Keep taking paid sill repair shifts while fit
Use AI measurements with physical wall checks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because robots could reach window work by 2031 while Niko and I have only three weeks saved. A paid inspection placement, real old-wall safety tests and reliable block dates would let me move before the account emptied.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who gets paid when a machine's neat new sill hides rot underneath. A failed repair comes back to a family living in that room, and somebody has to own the mistake.

headlineQuote: A failed repair comes back to a family living in that room, and somebody has to own the mistake.
portrait: Aisha is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level skill in window repair.
Her low wage, Niko's seasonal café hours and **three weeks saved** make gaps urgent.
She uses **AI every day**, checking its lists against chalk marks and old walls.
She seeks **paid inspection training** and local repair work without assuming retirement.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could remove essential window-fitting wages by the 2031 robot date.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **paid inspection placement**, old-wall safety trials and reliable block dates.
